source.title: Data Attribution of Emergent Misalignment with Persona Features
source.authors: C. Vetter; David Kaczér; Lucie Flek; Florian Mai

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether SAE-recovered features in open-weight LLMs relate to behavior, using model diffing and causal activation steering rather than the original toy-network method. It does not test superposition geometry itself.
record.gate_note: The study reports SAE feature shifts and steering outcomes that bear on V4. It does not measure overlapping directions, feature sparsity or importance as determinants of geometry, polysemanticity, or one-dimensional versus multidimensional feature structure. Its discussion of superposition geometry cites other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows. The document-attribution fine-tuning experiments address whether particular data induce emergent misalignment, not the claim’s representation geometry.
record.test_reason: The study uses pre-trained, off-the-shelf SAEs as a tool to study emergent misalignment (EM) through model diffing, steering and data attribution. It never tests whether SAEs recover the model's sparse features: no reconstruction, sparsity or interpretability checks, and no comparison against neurons. It tests nothing on overlapping directions, capacity, polysemanticity or feature dimensionality. Its results are about EM: which features shift, which steer EM, and which documents activate them. Steering success shows that certain decoder directions affect behaviour. It does not show that models contain sparse features in superposition. Superposition geometry appears only in a citation (Minegishi et al., 2026).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, but incomplete. The authors also report that steering re-aligns misaligned models in reverse, to MR as low as about 1%. They also report that synthetic pairs seeded from attributed documents induce significantly more EM than pairs seeded from random documents (CMH odds ratio 2.32). From this they conclude that the attributed content contributes the larger share of the effect, beyond format alone.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE model diffing and activation steering on open-weight LLMs, not the original toy-network setup. It does not reproduce the original superposition intervention or geometry measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports substantially weaker steering effects outside the main analyzed layers; it says a systematic search across layers was not computationally feasible. Steering strengths vary by model family.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding single SAE decoder directions to the residual stream induces coherent EM: up to 62.08% MR in Gemma 3 27B. About 20% of candidate features succeed. Random features from the same shifted pool almost never induce EM (0.06–0.20% mean best MR).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual SAE dictionary directions in LLMs can causally control high-level behavioural dispositions under steering.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning shifts only a minority of SAE features (7–27%), with a long-tailed shift distribution. The size of a feature's shift does not correlate with its steering effectiveness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning changes are concentrated in a small subset of SAE features, but a feature's activation shift does not predict its causal effect.

record.problems: The study relies heavily on an LLM judge and a small set of open-ended evaluation questions, and the authors note that results may be sensitive to these choices. Feature selection and categorization involve generated explanations and manual inspection. Steering is restricted to selected features and analyzed layers. The SAE features are not evidence here of complete or canonical units, and the study does not establish that retrieved proxy-corpus documents were in the models’ pre-training data.

untested.parts: Toy networks, sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry are not studied.
Capacity competition and polysemanticity are not studied.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure is not studied.
Spreading of features across neurons is not measured, and SAE recovery quality is not evaluated. Off-the-shelf SAEs are used as given.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not tested.
One-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: This is an EM paper that uses SAEs as a tool. The reader's T2/tests classification and V4 labels are not justified: the steering results bear on EM mechanisms, not on superposition or on whether SAEs recover sparse features. The only reference to superposition geometry is cited work (Minegishi et al., 2026). Row r3 misattributes Table 4's Gemma 2 top feature, which is #101487, not #91914.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy-network superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or polysemanticity.
Does not test whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
Tests SAE-recovered features in four LLMs, including their shifts and steering effects. Does not measure whether features spread across neurons.
Does not establish that SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: four models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; Gemma 2 9B Instruct; Gemma 3 27B Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE feature activation shifts under aligned and misaligned fine-tuning.
rows.measure: Share of SAE features with non-zero activation shifts
rows.value: 7–27%, averaged over the three fine-tuning domains, display a non-zero activation shift under either aligned or misaligned fine-tuning; shifts are long-tailed.
rows.note: The paper also reports that a small fraction of features accounts for most of the total shift. This is SAE feature measurement, not a measurement of feature overlap or neuron sharing.
rows.check: This measures how fine-tuning shifts SAE feature activations (7–27% of features shift). It does not measure whether the model holds sparse features or spreads features across neurons, so it does not bear on V4.

rows.subject: Gemma 3 27B Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Positive activation steering of a selected SAE feature in the aligned baseline model.

conditions.value: best coherent misalignment rate under IR ≤ 10%

rows.note: The paper reports this as the strongest steering case and says it exceeds the maximum MR of 35% achieved after misalignment fine-tuning.
rows.check: This is a selection value: the best-of-sweep misalignment rate (MR) under IR ≤ 10% for a feature chosen by hand. It measures the EM effect of the study's own method, not superposition.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Positive activation steering of a selected SAE feature in the aligned baseline model.

conditions.value: best coherent misalignment rate under IR ≤ 10%

rows.value: MR = 35.00% in Table 4; Appendix Table 11 reports MR = 35.88% and IR = 3.53%.
rows.note: The paper gives inconsistent MR values for this feature in its overview and appendix.
rows.check: This is a selection value and conflates two features. Table 4 lists Gemma 2's top feature as #101487 at 35.00%, while #91914 is 35.88% in Table 11. The row attributes the Table 4 value to #91914.
